# Town statistics summary

*Generated by `pipeline/build_stats.py` on 2026-10-18. Do not edit by hand; rerun the pipeline.*

> FairAssess NJ is an independent student research project that uses public data. It is not legal, tax, or appraisal advice. Homeowners file and present their own appeals. Confirm deadlines, fees, and forms with the Bergen County Board of Taxation.

This page sums up the town statistics for Bergen County single-family homes. It uses 3,806 clean sales with deeds recorded July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026 (rule T0). Rule IDs refer to `docs/methodology.md`. The full tables are `data/processed/town_stats.csv`, `town_tiers.csv`, and `county_summary.json`.

## What the measures mean

- **Assessment ratio**: assessed value divided by sale price. A home assessed at $400,000 that sold for $500,000 has a ratio of 80%.
- **Median ratio**: the middle ratio in a town. It is the typical share of market value the town assesses at.
- **COD (coefficient of dispersion)**: how far, on average, each home's ratio is from the median, as a percent. Lower means more even. IAAO's guideline for older, mixed suburbs is 15 or less.
- **PRD (price-related differential)**: the average ratio divided by the value-weighted average ratio. Above 1 means cheaper homes tend to have higher ratios. IAAO's range is 0.98 to 1.03.
- **PRB (price-related bias)**: about how much the ratio changes each time a home's value doubles. -0.05 means the ratio falls about 5% per doubling. IAAO's range is -0.05 to +0.05.
- **95% range**: the span where the true value most likely falls, given how many sales a town has. Small towns have wide ranges.
- **Value quarter**: each town's sales split into 4 equal groups, from lowest to highest value. Value here is the same mix PRB uses: half the sale price and half the assessment, turned back into a market value (rule T3).
- **Chapter 123 limits**: each year the state sets a range around each town's average ratio (about 15% above and below it). A home assessed above the upper limit may have grounds for an appeal. Ratios above 100% count as 100%.
- **Regressive pattern**: cheaper homes are assessed at a higher share of their value than expensive homes. A town gets this label when PRD is above 1.03 **and** PRB is below -0.05 (rule T5).

## Countywide results

Bergen towns assess at very different levels (the state's 2027 average ratios run from 47.06% in Garfield to 119.50% in Rockleigh; 2027CH123.pdf), so we report two versions. **The within-town version is the headline.** It divides each sale by its own town's median first, so it only measures unevenness inside towns.

| Measure | Within towns (headline) | All sales pooled (reference) |
|---|---|---|
| Sales | 3,806 | 3,806 |
| Median ratio | 1.000 (by design) | 61.4% (60.4% to 62.4%) |
| COD | 11.9 (11.6 to 12.3) | 24.7 (24.1 to 25.2) |
| PRD | 1.009 (1.004 to 1.015) | 1.005 (0.998 to 1.013) |
| PRB | 0.001 (-0.006 to 0.009) | 0.090 (0.077 to 0.103) |

Numbers in parentheses are 95% ranges.

## Towns in each label

| Label | Towns |

| Regressive pattern | 2 |
| Progressive pattern | 1 |
| Within standards | 28 |
| Mixed signals | 17 |
| Not enough sales | 22 |

- 48 towns have 20 or more sales and get a rank. 22 towns have under 20 sales, so their statistics are hidden. 21 of those are on the county's 2026 revaluation list (labeled "Recent revaluation"; see rule C9).
- Of the 48 ranked towns, 43 meet the IAAO COD guideline, 44 meet the PRD range, and 29 meet the PRB range.
- In 9 ranked towns the whole 95% PRB range is below 0, and in 4 it is above 0. In 1 the whole range is outside -0.10 to +0.10, which IAAO calls an "unacceptable" vertical inequity.
- 12 ranked towns change label when outliers are trimmed at 1.5 x IQR instead of 3.0: Cliffside Park, Bergenfield, Emerson, Tenafly, Hackensack, Park Ridge, Saddle Brook, Waldwick, Palisades Park, Englewood, Englewood Cliffs, North Arlington. Their town pages will say the result is sensitive to outliers.

## Sold homes outside the Chapter 123 limits, by value quarter (rule T7)

This adds up 24 towns with 20 or more sales, using each town's tax year 2027 limits (2027CH123.pdf). Towns on the 2027 revaluation list are left out, because Chapter 123 does not apply there in 2027 (rule K14). A sold home "above the upper limit" had a ratio high enough that, if its owner had the same numbers, they may have had grounds to appeal. This describes sold homes only. It is not a result for any one home.

| Value quarter | Sales | Above the upper limit | Below the lower limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (lowest value) | 304 | 43 (14.1%) | 75 (24.7%) |
| 2 | 297 | 30 (10.1%) | 84 (28.3%) |
| 3 | 293 | 21 (7.2%) | 81 (27.6%) |
| 4 (highest value) | 287 | 36 (12.5%) | 60 (20.9%) |

More sold homes fall below the lower limit than above the upper one. That is expected: the state's average ratio covers more than single-family homes, and our single-family median ratio is usually below it (methodology V3). So the limits sit a little high for single-family homes.

## Labeled towns and the 2027 revaluations

Towns on the county's 2027 revaluation list get new assessments for tax year 2027. Our numbers use the assessments from before that change. Labeled towns on that list: Bergenfield (Regressive pattern), Cliffside Park (Regressive pattern), Englewood (Progressive pattern). Their town pages should say the pattern describes the old assessments.

## Why quarters use value, not sale price

If we split homes by sale price instead, homes that happened to sell cheap would land in the lowest quarter *and* get a high ratio for the same reason. That makes towns look more regressive than they are. In this data, sorting by sale price gives the lowest quarter a higher median ratio than the highest quarter in 36 of 48 towns (median gap 5.7 points). Sorting by value does so in 22 of 48 (median gap -0.5 points), which agrees with PRB. Both versions are in `town_tiers.csv` (`tier_basis`).

## How to talk about these results

- Say a town "shows a regressive pattern in this data." Do not say a town "is unfair" or "is breaking the law."
- Labels use the point estimates (rule T5). Many small towns have wide 95% ranges, so check the range before making a strong claim.
- "Limited data" towns have 20 to 39 sales. Treat their numbers with extra care.
